    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Delta Air Lines has fallen behind United Airlines in terms of its transpacific network in recent years, but the Atlanta-based carrier has started to close that gap. This year, it reinstated flights between Los Angeles and Hong Kong, and next year it is reinstating its nonstop services between Seattle and Tokyo Narita, and also launching flights to Manila.

    Industry observers note that the airline is now preparing to announce yet another addition to its network next week. The SkyTeam member is hosting a major event in Seattle on December 2, where it is set to unveil at least one new route. It is widely expected to be Singapore, which it last served in 2019 via Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT).

    Industry observers note that delta has been planning a return to the Lion City for some time. As Simple Flying reported in August, the airline's Chief Commercial Officer, Joe Esposito, confirmed that Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) was part of its future network looks. There has since been further evidence that the service could launch as early as next year.

    Evidently, according to View From The Wing, the Atlanta-based airline identified Singapore as one of its newly introduced markets for 2027 in a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group. The airline stated in the presentation, “New markets unveiled for 2027 are Manila and Singapore.”.

    The service is expected to operate from the airline's West Coast hub at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) and would have an estimated block time of around 17 hours. Delta will likely deploy its Airbus A350-900 on the route, although the larger A350-1000 could eventually take over the service.

    Based on what is known so far, the service could launch in the summer or fall of 2027. Delta previously indicated that its Singapore service would follow the launch of its Los Angeles–Manila route. The latter is scheduled to commence on March 28, 2027, initially operating three times weekly before increasing to daily on June 7.

    It has been revealed that singapore was once part of an extensive connecting network through Tokyo that Delta inherited from Northwest Airlines. When the carrier decided to withdraw from the Singapore market, it cited financial pressure on the route. Growing nonstop capacity between the US and Singapore, stronger brand loyalty towards local carriers, and competition from Star Alliance members at Changi made it increasingly difficult for Delta to compete.

    Recent findings suggest that but the proposed service would put Delta in direct competition with Singapore Airlines. According to scheduled data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, the Singaporean flag carrier operates five weekly flights between Seattle and Singapore. It also dominates the wider US–Singapore market, as noted above in the table. Meanwhile, United Airlines is at the moment the only US carrier serving Singapore nonstop, operating twice daily from San Francisco.

    It is interesting to see Delta expanding its presence in Asia. Its overall capacity in Asia is up around 5.8% this year compared to 2025. As noted earlier, there have been several interesting developments in its transpacific network. In June, the airline reinstated daily flights between its Southern California hub and Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) after decades of absence on the route.

    Notably, it also marked its return to Hong Kong for the first time since 2018. From March 27, 2027, the airline will resume daily flights between Seattle and Tokyo Narita for the first time since March 2020, complementing its existing service to Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND). Elsewhere, it will make its debut in the Philippines market.

    Sources indicate that while not part of its regular network, the SkyTeam member has also scheduled a handful of nonstop flights to and from Las Vegas Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) for the upcoming Consumer Electronics Show (CES). These include flights between Las Vegas and Hong Kong on January 4 and 10, and between Las Vegas and Taipei on January 5 and 10.

    Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S.
    • Recent findings suggest that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    Recent findings suggest that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., remarked the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    In a recent development, “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting newly introduced technologies and gaps between sectors,” she noted in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

    The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    It has been revealed that the House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    Recent findings suggest that senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH.
    • On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA).
    • It has been revealed that flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. While this is still being investigated, there’s a theory as to what happened, given what all passengers had in common….

    On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA). Both flights were operated by the Airbus A330-900neo, with as many as 620 passengers onboard.

    It has been revealed that flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday. The flights had one thing in common, which is that between them, dozens of passengers became ill.

    The illnesses onboard were so bad that a “MANV 25” response was triggered at Frankfurt Airport. That’s a German emergency response alert for a mass casualty incident — “Massenanfall von Verletzten” (though fortunately there were no fatalities here).

    Passengers onboard were screened by medical teams, and one person on each flight was taken to a local hospital, while others are being monitored.

    It’s not uncommon to hear stories of multiple people becoming sick on flights. Sometimes it’s a fume event, sometimes it could be a case of food poisoning (though it doesn’t usually happen that fast), etc. So what’s going on here, that people on two separate Condor flights became ill?

    Well, the passengers on these two flights had one thing in common — they all came off the AidaBella cruise ship in La Romana, and then these flights were sold as part of the cruise package.

    So while this is still being investigated, a norovirus outbreak on the cruise ship is believed to be the likely culprit. I’ve gotta say, an airplane seems like a pretty unpleasant place to come down with a gastrointestinal illness, so I imagine the lavatory situation onboard probably wasn’t great.

    Dozens of passengers on two separate Condor flights between the Dominican Republic and Germany around the same time became ill, triggering an emergency response at Frankfurt Airport, which included a couple of people being hospitalized.

    While it remains to be seen what caused this, the belief is that it could be some sort of a norovirus outbreak, based on the symptoms, as well as the fact that the passengers had all come off the same cruise ship. I hope everyone makes a quick recovery.

    • Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways at the moment has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, in the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds. The airline will be introducing a “mini-Qsuite” type product on these planes, and we’ve now learned exactly when this new premium narrow body jet will enter service.

    Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways at the moment has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order. This includes 10 A321LRs and 40 A321neos — both of those are latest generation aircraft, with the A321LR featuring additional range.

    In a recent development, the expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026. The 10 A321LRs should join the fleet pretty quickly, and will then be followed by the A321neos. The A321LRs will be configured with 160 seats, including 16 business class seats and 144 economy class seats.

    According to recent reports, the A321LR has a maximum range of 4,000 nautical miles, so it can be used for many destinations in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Below is a map showing the rough range from Doha (though in reality it won’t be quite as far, accounting for winds, fuel reserves, etc.).

    Now, for those paying close attention, I should acknowledge that Qatar Airways briefly flew six leased, all-economy A321neos, but those were just intended as a temporary solution, and are now flying for Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is running an interesting operation.

    Qatar Airways’ A321neo-family aircraft order goes back a long time, and involved a lot of drama. The order was first announced in 2011, then the airline reconfirmed and upsized it in 2017. However, then former Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker got into a fight with Airbus over A350 production quality, and refused to take delivery of any Airbus planes.

    That turned into a massive court battle, which was eventually resolved. But in the process, Qatar Airways lost all of its Airbus delivery slots, which is why these planes are coming way later than initially expected.

    Recent findings suggest that qatar Airways has been promising all along that it would introduce some sort of a next generation flat bed business class product on its Airbus A321LRs. As you’d expect, business class seats on narrow bodies sometimes differ from those on wide bodies, due to differing cabin constraints.

    It has been revealed that what can we expect onboard these Qatar Airways A321LRs in business class? Executive Traveller quotes Qatar Airways CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater as saying that the fresh business class product will be based on the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform.

    These planes will boast 16 business class seats, in a 1-1 configuration. This product offers reverse herringbone seats, and Qatar Airways aims to have doors at each seat as well, of course with its customized finishes.

    Industry observers note that the launch customer for the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform was Air France on its A350s. However, that’s the wide body version of the seat, which is modified from the narrow body version.

    When it comes to the narrow body version of the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, ITA Airways was the launch customer, on its A321neos.

    This is also the product that Etihad is installing on its A321LRs. ITA Airways and Etihad don’t have doors in business class, but Qatar Airways does proposal to offer it. Etihad also markets the first row of the cabin as first class (and that has doors), but I wouldn’t expect Qatar Airways to do something similar.

    This is about as good as narrow body business class seats get, as it’s generally preferred to the herringbone seats you’ll find on other carriers, like JetBlue A321LRs, American A321XLRs, etc.

    Qatar Airways now seems pretty certain about the delivery of its upcoming Airbus A321LRs, as the airline has officially put the first routes on sale, as flagged by AeroRoutes:.

    When you pull up the above flights, you’ll now see the seat map for the A321LR, which confirms the 16-seat business class cabin.

    In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first of 10 Airbus A321LRs. This will be the first custom designed next generation narrow body that the airline takes delivery of. We knew the airline would offer flat bed seats on these planes, and now we have the details of that.

    It has been revealed that the airline has gone with the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, the same product you’ll find on similar planes of Etihad and ITA Airways. However, unlike those airlines, Qatar Airways will have doors in business class. The planes will enter service by very early 2027, flying from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich.

    Latest Update: American Blocking Domestic Saver Awards Close To Departure (Within Six Days)

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major newly introduced restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).
    • With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure.
    • Sources indicate that historically, American has been by far the best of the “big three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major newly introduced restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).

    With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure. Initially, all domestic nonstop saver awards within six days of departure were pulled. In recent days, it looks like American has expanded this to all domestic connecting itineraries as well, so I’d like to cover those details (thanks to azbobcat for flagging this).

    Sources indicate that historically, American has been by far the best of the “big three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights. American actually releases a good amount of saver award seats across cabins, and it’s one of the things that makes AAdvantage better than the competition.

    Sources indicate that however, in May 2026, we saw American introduce a major change to how it releases award space to partner frequent flyer programs. Long story short, American started blocking all nonstop, domestic saver award availability, for flights within six days (exactly 144 hours) of departure.

    As soon as a flight gets to the point where it’s 144 hours until departure, you’ll see that the airline “turns off” its saver fare classes — I’m referring specifically to the “U” (saver business class award) and “T” (saver economy award) fare classes, which show up when searching on ExpertFlyer, for example.

    Industry observers note that initially, this applied exclusively to nonstop, domestic award tickets, as connecting itineraries and all international itineraries (including short haul international ones) weren’t impacted by this. However, this seems to have now expanded to domestic connecting itineraries as well.

    So any wholly domestic itinerary exclusively on American is no longer bookable at the saver level within six days of departure. International itineraries continue to be bookable within six days of departure, whether traveling nonstop or with a connection.

    What would cause American to suddenly “shut off” saver awards for domestic routes within days of departure?

    Industry observers note that what’s interesting here is that the implications for AAdvantage members are limited. Yes, American has shut off awards in the saver fare classes, but that’s not to say that American isn’t making reasonably priced awards available within days of departure. American has long used some kind of dynamic award pricing concept for its own flights, regardless of whether or not there’s saver availability.

    It’s just that any awards in the official saver fare buckets aren’t available, and therefore aren’t bookable with points belonging to partner programs.

    Sources indicate that so it sure seems to me that the intent here is to block award availability for those booking through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club. It goes without saying that I absolutely hate this restriction, as someone who “funds” a vast majority of my domestic American travel using Atmos Rewards points. At the same time, I also have to say that I can’t blame American for this change, as the airline has just made it too easy.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve been booking basically all my travel directly into American first class using Atmos Rewards points — I just set ExpertFlyer availability alerts for “U” class, it opens up a vast majority of the time, and then I book. It’s not surprising that American finally got a bit savvier.

    American is now blocking all saver awards within exactly six days of departure for all domestic itineraries. This means within that timeframe, there’s no “U” or “T” availability, which corresponds to the saver business and economy award fare buckets, respectively. Initially this only applied to nonstop flights, while now it also applies to connecting itineraries.

    In a recent development, for American AAdvantage members, the implications are limited, since American can still make reasonably priced awards available, just not formally in those fare buckets. The practical implications here are that partner programs just don’t have access to these award seats close to departure anymore.

    What do you make of American’s six day rule on award tickets?

    #88344. Industry News: FAA Bans Line Up And Wait Operations “Forever,” With Even More Delays Expected

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (845 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: FAA Bans Line Up And Wait Operations “Forever,” With Even More Delays Expected

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (845 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has introduced stricter requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations at airports across the United States, effective November 24, 2026.
    • In a recent development, despite reports describing the measure as a permanent nationwide ban, the FAA has not prohibited Line Up and Wait operations altogether.
    • The newly introduced requirement is outlined in FAA Notice JO 7210.979, which mandates that a standalone watch supervision position must be staffed whenever Line Up and Wait operations are conducted.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has introduced stricter requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations at airports across the United States, effective November 24, 2026. The new rules require a dedicated air traffic control supervisor to oversee these operations, potentially preventing controllers at understaffed facilities from using the procedure. The change comes just as millions of Americans prepare to travel for Thanksgiving, raising concerns about longer departure queues and additional flight delays.

    In a recent development, despite reports describing the measure as a permanent nationwide ban, the FAA has not prohibited Line Up and Wait operations altogether. Instead, it has made them conditional on additional staffing, introducing another operational challenge for an air traffic control system already struggling with personnel shortages.

    The newly introduced requirement is outlined in FAA Notice JO 7210.979, which mandates that a standalone watch supervision position must be staffed whenever Line Up and Wait operations are conducted. Previously, the relevant guidance recommended that the local control position should not be combined with other responsibilities. The updated wording makes this a mandatory requirement, meaning supervisors can no longer simultaneously perform other operational duties while overseeing these operations.

    Line Up and Wait is a widely used air traffic control procedure that allows aircraft to enter an assigned runway and hold in position while waiting for takeoff clearance. It helps improve runway efficiency because departing aircraft are already positioned when the runway becomes available. However, under the fresh requirements, airports without sufficient personnel to provide dedicated supervision will have to keep aircraft waiting at taxiway holding points instead. This could reduce departure capacity, particularly during busy periods.

    According to recent reports, the timing is concerning because November 24 coincides with the beginning of one of America's busiest Thanksgiving travel periods. According to the FAA forecast reported by Traveling for Business, more than 52,000 flights were scheduled for that Tuesday, with over 417,000 expected throughout the nine-day holiday period.

    FAA provided a statement to Simple Flying to clarify the latest rule:.

    The FAA is taking proactive steps to further strengthen runway safety by enhancing staffing and supervisory requirements for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) at airports nationwide, effective Nov. 24, 2026. These measures ensure dedicated controller staffing and supervisory oversight during LUAW operations and reinforce the FAA’s commitment to maintaining the highest safety standards. This will not impact airport operations.

    Dedicated Local Control: The local control position responsible for arriving and departing aircraft must not be combined with any non-local control position.

    Recent findings suggest that stand-Alone Watch Supervision: A dedicated watch supervision position must be staffed and cannot be combined with any other position. This strengthens existing guidance by making stand-alone watch supervision mandatory.

    The controversy gained attention after a radio exchange at Albuquerque International Sunport (ABQ). According to TheTravel, a controller told a Southwest Airlines crew about the fresh nationwide requirement, warning it could slow departures during the busiest travel time of the Thanksgiving rush. The controller described the restriction as something that would last forever, although the FAA's official notice did not use that wording.

    Industry observers note that importantly, the FAA's stated objective is to improve runway safety, not reduce airport capacity. Having a dedicated supervisor overseeing operations should help prevent distractions and improve situational awareness when aircraft are positioned on active runways. The FAA's existing procedures also emphasize that Line Up and Wait is not takeoff clearance and that aircraft should not normally remain in that position for more than 90 seconds without further instructions.

    Sources indicate that but there is also an key clarification: the official notice lists June 9, 2027, as its cancellation date. Therefore, describing the measure as an indefinite or permanent prohibition is misleading. The actual impact will depend on staffing levels at individual towers and how frequently they can provide the additional supervisory position.

    According to recent reports, the FAA is attempting to address its longstanding air traffic controller shortage through an ambitious recruitment campaign, including an unusual effort to attract video gamers. In October 2026, the agency declared that it had hired 2,235 controller trainees during the fiscal year, exceeding its recruitment target. The campaign reportedly attracted more than 12,000 qualified applicants within just 24 hours, demonstrating the potential of targeting candidates with strong multitasking and decision-making abilities.

    However, recruiting additional candidates does not immediately solve the staffing problem. According to the FAA's 2026 workforce proposal, becoming a fully certified controller can take more than two years, depending on the complexity of the assigned facility. The agency has set recruitment targets of 2,300 trainees for fiscal year 2027 and 2,400 for 2028, while expanding training capacity and modernizing its workforce management procedures.

    As a result, the fresh Line Up and Wait requirements could create additional operational pressure before the benefits of increased recruitment become apparent. Although the measure is intended to strengthen runway safety, airports with limited staffing may have fewer opportunities to use an efficiency-enhancing procedure. For Thanksgiving travelers, the immediate concern is that an already busy aviation network could face additional departure bottlenecks during the holiday rush.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees).
    • It has been revealed that in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

    It has been revealed that in my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.

    Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:.

    Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most important factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

    According to recent reports, in terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who right now has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    Sources indicate that for a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    It has been revealed that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    According to recent reports, now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only fresh rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

    According to recent reports, $99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

    The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

    As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:.

    Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

    Sources indicate that rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Sources indicate that starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    It has been revealed that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

    In a recent development, southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

    Industry observers note that another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

    Sources indicate that each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

    In a recent development, on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

    Recent findings suggest that as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

    Recent findings suggest that the Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Sources indicate that one of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

    The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

    You’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up quickly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

    However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

    If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

    You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:.

    Industry observers note that there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

    The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:.

    So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

    Recent findings suggest that if you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:.

    The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

    The Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

    This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

    In a recent development, starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

    I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

    Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

    Stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

    I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an matter using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

    I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

    According to recent reports, I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

    Sources indicate that as such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to New York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

    Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

    Industry observers note that neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

    It has been revealed that as a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

    It has been revealed that I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

    For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

    Industry observers note that my experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this….

    Sources indicate that I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

    I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

    I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

    #88339. How The Airbus A350 Survives Environmental Stress During The Longest Flights In The World

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1715 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    How The Airbus A350 Survives Environmental Stress During The Longest Flights In The World

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before entering commercial service, the Airbus A350 had to prove it could withstand some of the harshest conditions on Earth.
    • Through these trials, Airbus sought to ensure that the A350 could operate safely and reliably across a wide range of environments.
    • It has been revealed that before entering commercial service, every upcoming aircraft must undergo extensive testing and certification to demonstrate compliance with aviation safety standards.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before entering commercial service, the Airbus A350 had to prove it could withstand some of the harshest conditions on Earth. Airbus needed to establish how its engines, systems, and structure would respond to extreme temperatures and demanding operating conditions. From the freezing Canadian Arctic to the scorching deserts of the United Arab Emirates and the high-altitude airports of Bolivia, Airbus deliberately pushed its new widebody aircraft to its limits.

    Through these trials, Airbus sought to ensure that the A350 could operate safely and reliably across a wide range of environments. The A350 has since become a key aircraft for ultra-long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop flights between Singapore and New York. So, how did Airbus test the A350, and what did these trials reveal about the aircraft's capabilities?

    It has been revealed that before entering commercial service, every upcoming aircraft must undergo extensive testing and certification to demonstrate compliance with aviation safety standards. For Airbus aircraft, the main certification authority is the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), while the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) validates the design for the US market. The process begins with the Type Certificate (TC), which confirms that an aircraft's design meets the applicable airworthiness requirements. Manufacturers must also hold the relevant production approvals, while each individual aircraft requires a Certificate of Airworthiness (CoA) before entering service. Airlines must additionally meet operational requirements, including crew training, maintenance arrangements, and any necessary authorizations.

    Sources indicate that the certification process also varies depending on the aircraft's design and available configurations. For example, Airbus' A320neo Family certification program covered six airframe and engine combinations. The A319neo, A320neo and A321neo each required validation of their airframes, systems and two available engine options: the CFM International LEAP-1A and Pratt & Whitney Geared Turbofan (GTF). These campaigns also verified whether the aircraft met their performance targets for fuel consumption and range, reflecting improvements from the upcoming engines and Sharklet wingtip devices.

    In a recent development, for the A350-900, Airbus completed its flight-test and certification campaign in just over 14 months, setting an industry record for the program's completion time. Five test aircraft accumulated more than 2,600 flight hours, during which Airbus evaluated the aircraft's handling characteristics, systems, performance, and reliability. The campaign culminated in the A350-900 receiving Type Certification from EASA and the FAA in 2014. However, the program also involved specialized environmental testing in Canada, the United Arab Emirates, and Bolivia, along with controlled temperature trials at the McKinley Climatic Laboratory in the United States. These tests would establish how the A350 performed in conditions far beyond those encountered during routine airline operations.

    It has been revealed that in January 2014, Airbus took its A350-900 MSN3 development aircraft to Iqaluit, Canada, to conduct cold-weather trials in temperatures as low as -28°C. A team of 48 Airbus specialists assessed how the aircraft's engines and systems performed in freezing conditions. One key test involved starting the engines and auxiliary power unit (APU) after a cold soak, during which the aircraft was left exposed to extremely low temperatures for an extended period. The team also conducted system checks, low-speed taxiing, rejected takeoffs, and a local test flight to verify the aircraft's performance.

    Three years later, Airbus returned to Iqaluit with the larger A350-1000, which underwent five days of intensive ground and flight testing in temperatures ranging from -28°C to -37°C. Alongside these Arctic trials, Airbus also used the McKinley Climatic Laboratory at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida, becoming the first Airbus aircraft to undergo testing at the facility. Unlike Iqaluit, where engineers depended on natural weather, the laboratory's climate-controlled hangar allowed Airbus to simulate temperatures from -40°C to +40°C under controlled conditions.

    However, extreme cold was only one part of the A350's environmental testing program. While the Canadian trials focused on the aircraft's ability to operate in freezing conditions, Airbus also needed to assess its performance in extreme heat and at high-altitude airports. This took the A350 to Al Ain in the United Arab Emirates and La Paz in Bolivia, where high temperatures and reduced air density presented a different set of operational challenges.

    While freezing temperatures presented one challenge, Airbus also needed to demonstrate that the A350 could operate safely in extreme heat. In July 2017, the manufacturer sent its A350-1000 test aircraft, MSN065, to Al Ain International Airport in the United Arab Emirates for a three-day hot-weather testing campaign. Conducted between 4 and 7 July, the trials exposed the aircraft to temperatures exceeding 40°C, reaching as high as 48°C. The objective was to assess how the aircraft's systems performed in scorching conditions, particularly the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and cabin air-conditioning systems.

    According to recent reports, one main concern was whether the aircraft could maintain comfortable cabin temperatures on the ground, where cooling systems must cope with intense external heat. Engineers also assessed engine performance, as higher temperatures reduce air density and affect engine thrust and takeoff performance. This can increase the runway distance required for departure, particularly at airports with shorter runways. The importance of these limitations became evident in June 2017, when extreme temperatures in Phoenix, Arizona, led to dozens of flight cancellations involving regional aircraft with lower maximum operating temperature limits.

    According to Airbus, the A350-1000 successfully met all the parameters established for its Al Ain campaign, demonstrating its readiness to operate in extreme heat. However, high temperatures are not the only factor that reduces air density. Airports situated thousands of meters above sea level present similar performance challenges, even when outside temperatures are considerably lower. To assess these conditions, Airbus also conducted high-altitude testing in Bolivia.

    Airbus also took the A350 to El Alto International Airport in La Paz, Bolivia, situated approximately 4,061 meters (13,325 feet) above sea level. At this elevation, air density is roughly 40% lower than at sea level under comparable standard conditions, creating significant challenges for aircraft performance. Thinner air reduces the amount of oxygen available to the engines, limiting the thrust they can produce, while also reducing the lift generated by the wings at a given airspeed. Consequently, aircraft generally require higher true airspeeds and longer take-off distances to become airborne.

    High-altitude testing allows Airbus to evaluate how aircraft systems and engines respond to these demanding conditions. One particularly notable assessment involves engine starting, which becomes more challenging as air density decreases. Engineers also examine thrust response, takeoff and climb performance, and the aircraft's handling characteristics. Jean-Philippe Cottet, Airbus' head of design development flight tests, identified starting engines at high altitude as one of the main reasons the manufacturer conducts trials specifically in La Paz.

    The A350-900 and A350-1000 were among the aircraft Airbus tested at La Paz, which has also hosted other Airbus development programs. These evaluations help establish the aircraft's operational limitations and demonstrate its ability to perform safely at high-elevation airports. Together with the cold-weather trials in Canada and hot-weather testing in the UAE, the campaign provided evidence of the A350's capabilities across markedly different operating environments.

    Sources indicate that beyond extreme weather testing, Airbus also needed to demonstrate how the A350 would perform during extended commercial operations. As part of its certification campaign, the manufacturer conducted a global route-proving program, visiting 14 major airports across four separate trips and covering approximately 81,700 nautical miles in 180 flight hours. Airbus also introduced an Early Long Flights (ELF) program, which went beyond regulatory certification requirements. These simulated commercial services carried Airbus employees acting as passengers, with airline flight crews operating a fully equipped cabin to evaluate onboard systems under realistic conditions. Such testing helped prepare the A350 for demanding long-haul operations, including Singapore Airlines' nonstop services between Singapore and Upcoming York, which use the A350-900ULR and can exceed 18 hours.

    It has been revealed that the A350's long-range capabilities are also central to Qantas' Project Sunrise, which aims to introduce nonstop flights from Sydney to London and New York using specially configured A350-1000ULR aircraft. Compared with the standard A350-1000, the Project Sunrise variant incorporates an additional fuel tank with approximately 5,283 gallons (20,000 liters) of capacity to support longer journeys. The A350's composite fuselage also resists corrosion and fatigue, while its cabin pressurization and environmental control systems allow a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet and higher humidity than many older aircraft. These features are particularly relevant on flights lasting 18 hours or more, where passenger comfort becomes increasingly important.

    However, the ability to withstand extreme temperatures and remain airborne for extended periods is only part of the challenge. Ultra-long-haul operations also require careful management of crew fatigue, passenger wellbeing, maintenance schedules, and operational reliability. As airlines prepare to operate flights approaching 20 hours, the question is no longer simply how far an aircraft can fly, but rather how comfortably and efficiently passengers and crew can endure the journey.

    While the A350's certification trials demonstrated its ability to withstand extreme operating conditions, flights approaching 20 hours present another challenge: passenger wellbeing. Ahead of its Project Sunrise services, Qantas partnered with researchers from the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre to investigate ways of reducing jet lag on ultra-long-haul flights. During experimental flights lasting approximately 20 hours, researchers monitored 23 volunteers wearing tracking devices as they followed specially designed schedules for meals, cabin lighting, sleep, and movement. Initial findings suggested that passengers following these routines experienced less severe self-reported jet lag, better sleep quality during the flight and improved cognitive performance in the two days following arrival compared with those following conventional inflight routines.

    Sources indicate that qantas looks to incorporate these findings into its A350-1000ULR operations, including tailored cabin lighting, recommended meal and rest schedules, and a dedicated Wellbeing Zone where premium economy and economy passengers can stretch and move around. The airline also expects its nonstop Project Sunrise services to reduce total journey times by more than three hours compared with connecting flights. While Singapore Airlines' existing A350-900ULR operations have already demonstrated the aircraft family's suitability for ultra-long-haul services, Project Sunrise will provide another important test of its capabilities.

    Ultimately, the success of these routes will depend not only on aircraft reliability and commercial performance, but also on how effectively airlines can make journeys approaching 20 hours comfortable for passengers and manageable for crews.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.
    • Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

    Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

    “It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries mentioned at a press conference following the election.

    According to recent reports, while Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

    Sources indicate that “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”.

    Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

    Industry observers note that “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these challenges,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”.

    Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

    “This is the beginning of a newly introduced bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., stated at the press conference.

    In a recent development, rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

    According to recent reports, jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

    At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

    “We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

    “I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”.

    Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had noted they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

    Recent findings suggest that pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Recent findings suggest that the entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

    Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”.

    Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

    He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

    “House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he noted at his news conference.

    #88337. Industry News: When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1452 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1452 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question.
    • Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those).
    • The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices….

    Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

    The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

    Recent findings suggest that in most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

    However, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

    While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

    Recent findings suggest that broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

    I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

    Sources indicate that I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is presently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

    When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

    Industry observers note that it’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

    Cathay Pacific first class is exactly the opposite — the crews are spectacularly reactive. That might sound sarcastic, but it’s not. On Cathay Pacific you (hopefully) won’t see a flight attendant once between meal services without calling them, and that’s so that your privacy is maximized. But if you push the call button a flight attendant will cheerily appear within seconds.

    Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

    Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

    Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:.

    That being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

    The above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:.

    On US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes problem with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

    In a recent development, all airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no complications with using them for service.

    Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

    In a recent development, us airline here . I’m more than happy to take call lights in any cabin. When it gets concerning is when I customs keeps pressing it for alcohol refills . I have never heard crew members making an announcement that the call light is for emergency only , except when customer press it during taxi, take off , and landing.

    Who else ran to the comments to see how you crazy folk use the call button.

    I use it in business class if I'm done with a meal and am burried in the set table with plates and all. Without the call button the crew may not proactively come clear it for hours.

    If the airline offered complementary drinks, then no reason not to use it to ask for another. Just because they served you one doesn’t make a difference, there’s no cap on how many drinks are complementary so it’s part of the job. If the tray hasn’t been cleared and you need the bathroom. Yes you should feel comfortable calling the crew. If you want your meal early, that’s pushing it. You want an extra blanket? Maybe. You want to adjust the cabin temperature; I’d reserve this request for premium cabins, unless the temperature is ridiculous. Merely my opinion though, of course, now how it practically works - you will always get some cabin crew who don’t want to do extra work so even resent basic aspects of their job like serving drinks or clearing a table so you can, you know, get out of your seat to the bathroom - not really optional! I can see how this will play out totally differently in a cabin with 100 other passengers in close proximity.

    I do not care what cabin I’m travelling in, I’m pressing the button if I want something.

    IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

    Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

    In a recent development, just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

    IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:.

    Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

    For non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

    Keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand Newly introduced IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

    IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

    In a recent development, IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

    It has been revealed that there are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

    Allegiant Air Ditches 26 Nonstop Routes: See Full List Now

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
