    Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight: What your rights are in 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • Recent disruptions in U.S. air travel highlight the importance of understanding passenger refund rights.
  • Federal rules require airlines to issue refunds for canceled flights or significant delays if you choose not to travel, regardless of the cause.
  • A 'significant delay' is defined as three hours or more for domestic flights and six hours or more for international flights.
  • Refunds must be processed automatically and promptly—within seven days for credit card payments and 20 days for other payment methods.
  • Refund eligibility only applies if you decline rebooking and do not accept alternative compensation such as vouchers or miles.
  • Airlines are not required to provide compensation for meals, hotels or ground transportation unless the disruption is within their control.
  • Passengers can file a complaint with the Department of Transportation if they believe refund rules were not followed.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the matter is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • According to recent reports, “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the matter is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    According to recent reports, “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    At problem is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly mentioned it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they proposal to bring up a vote next year.

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump remarked, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    Sources indicate that “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the problem.

    “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

What a story this is!

    News On Japan has the story of how mileage running has caused problems for locals on some of Okinawa’s remote islands, as they’ve struggled to purchase Japan Airlines tickets due to a flood of mileage runners.

    While the story has been published in recent days, it seems to date back to February 2026 (best I can tell), when Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank program was offering double Life Status Points for flights. This promotion incentivized all domestic flights equally, so some savvy frequent flyers decided to seek out the shortest flights, so that they could cram in as many flights in a day as possible.

    It has been revealed that this ended up bringing them to Okinawa, where you’ll find some of the shortest flights in Japan Airlines’ system. These include flights between Ishigaki (ISG), Miyako (MMY), Naha (OKA), and Tarama (TRA). According to reports, some mileage runners booked up to a staggering 12 flights per day, leaving few empty seats on some essential flights.

    Sources indicate that at Miyako Airport, some passengers were observed arriving with just small handbags, and then immediately heading to the departures area to board their next flight. As a few travelers explained:.

    The problem is that this mileage running reportedly created serious difficulties for locals, who depend on the island flights for medical appointments, shopping, and other essential travel. There were some successive days in February where flights between Miyako and Tarama were booked out in advance, leaving locals unable to book seats. Here’s what some locals had to say:.

    Tarama Mayor Mitsuo Iranami even called on mileage runners to consider the impact their activities were having on the island community, commenting “I would like those doing mileage runs to understand the situation on remote islands and exercise some consideration, taking into account the number of people participating.”.

    Recent findings suggest that japan Airlines reportedly even introduced measures intended to counteract this, including offering full refunds without cancellation fees, along with 500 bonus miles as an incentive. Below is a news story in Japanese about this, so you can watch that with subtitles, if you’d like.

    Sources indicate that while it’s fairly common to see loyalty programs offer promotions, nowadays it’s rare to see deals that are actually that lucrative. When it does happen, we sometimes see that the people behind the promotion clearly didn’t think through all possible scenarios, and this is one of those situations.

    While Japan Airlines’ double status points promotion in February is pretty standard, the airline has added a newly introduced restriction for the offer this coming year, by capping the number of bonus points that can be earned during the promotion period, presumably to prevent something like this from happening.

    Obviously I feel bad for the locals in this situation, but it’s also hard to blame frequent flyers here for simply taking advantage of a promotion as advertised.

    Japan Airlines’ Mileage Bank frequent flyer program ran a promotion that might have just done too good of a job getting people to book flights, as a double Life Status Points offer caused some people to book up to a dozen flights per day, with some flights reportedly having up to 80% of passengers be mileage runners.

    Ordinarily that would be considered a success in terms of filling planes, but the problem here is that mileage runners descended on island routes that are also a lifeline for residents, given the efficiency of flying there. It’s not often you hear a mayor make a plea with mileage runners, but that’s exactly what happened here.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that delta Air Lines is throwing an Asian night market in Seattle on December 2, where they’ll finally reveal non-stop Singapore service.
    • Industry observers note that enilria reported the December 2 Seattle announcement several days ago and highlighted the invitation’s Asian theme.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that delta Air Lines is throwing an Asian night market in Seattle on December 2, where they’ll finally reveal non-stop Singapore service. That would put Delta into a roughly 17 hour nonstop fight with Singapore Airlines, giving its customers a way to reach one of Asia’s most crucial business centers without changing planes in Seoul. Enilria reported the December 2 Seattle announcement several days ago and highlighted the invitation’s Asian theme. Aviation watchdog JonNYC has now corroborated that direction, reporting that the event has an “Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme,” then adding: “Singapore as in.” Heard the Delta Seattle event has an Asian destination inspired holiday night market theme — JonNYC (@xJonNYC) November 23, 2026 The invitation is for Delta Night Market at MOPOP, Seattle’s Museum of Pop Culture, on Wednesday, December 2 from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. It promises food, drinks, shopping and cultural experiences built around Asian destinations, along with city-inspired charms guests can collect. The line that caught Enilria’s attention: Seven destinations. One unforgettable night. Delta’s current and unveiled East and Southeast Asian destinations are Tokyo, Seoul, Shanghai, Taipei, Hong Kong and Manila. That’s seven airports when you count both Tokyo Haneda and Narita, but six cities. If they’re counting cities, Singapore makes seven. So I don’t take this to mean seven new routes, though of course there may be additional routes announced. . And there’s a more concrete clue than the party theme. In a July 29 presentation to a Pacific air traffic coordination group, Delta wrote: New markets announced for 2027 are Manila and Singapore. This Has Been Coming For More Than A Year I reported Delta’s prepares to return to Singapore and Manila in October 2025. The following month, I wrote about their internal view that Europe was already pretty full, and that future long haul growth would lean heavily toward Asia, from both Los Angeles and Seattle. JonNYC has been all over this story. In August, Delta revealed at an event for its largest corporate customers that Singapore would follow closely behind Manila. Los Angeles–Manila is scheduled to begin March 28, 2027, initially three times weekly before going daily June 7. Delta last served Singapore in September 2019, as a flight from Tokyo Narita. They dismantled the connecting hub inherited from Northwest, moved their U.S.–Tokyo flying to Haneda and relied more heavily on Korean Air’s Seoul hub to get passengers elsewhere in Asia. Singapore Is A Market Delta Needs To Sell Singapore combines regional headquarters, finance, technology and a wealthy local market. For the multinational business traffic Delta wants, it has become more important than Hong Kong. There are now several times as many regional corporate headquarters in Singapore than Hong Kong.     #88313. Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

    Flydubai Resuming Israel Flights After Pilot Tried To Crash Plane Into Airport

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.
    • He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer.
    • Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

    He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

    Ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an revision, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

    The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

    This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss upcoming security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

    Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with latest steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:.

    According to recent reports, “The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the tech giant has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”.

    According to recent reports, tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

    Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG.

    Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

    Sources indicate that one of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

    Industry observers note that however, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

    I am curious if there were some latest policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

    It has been revealed that israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the plan is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

    Some new security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

    This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

    What do you make of flydubai resuming Israel flights?

    It has been revealed that in June 2025 he was flying United Airlines first class out of Houston. That December he was boarding American Airlines in Miami for St. Croix, standing in the boarding line with an escort.

    We could enjoy Jimmy Carter walking through a Delta Air Lines cabin and greeting passengers without agreeing about his presidency.

    Jimmy Carter greeting passengers aboard Delta Air Lines, June 8, 2017.

    According to recent reports, george W. Bush gets more room to be a retired president, too (sometimes more from Democrats than from Trump Republicans, given the split between Trump and the Bush family). Enjoying an encounter with a former president doesn’t require revising your assessment of his time in office.

    There are still airline complications worth arguing about. In June 2025, I criticized American Airlines bumping a passenger from first class to accommodate Biden on flight 2717 from Minneapolis to Philadelphia. He’d been attending the funeral of murdered Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman.

    A former president’s scheduling preferences shouldn’t outrank someone else’s confirmed seat. If the airline needs room for his party, it can ask for volunteers and pay them enough to take a different seat or flight. It seems President Trump, who already owned aircraft before entering office, may have an ex-Qatari royal 747 at his disposal. Hopefully better judgment will prevail there.

    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.
    • It has been revealed that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

    It has been revealed that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” mentioned Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking notable.”.

    It has been revealed that johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    According to recent reports, "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he remarked on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson stated Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    Recent findings suggest that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he mentioned.

    In a recent development, there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Industry observers note that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    Recent findings suggest that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a initiative in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle mentioned they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” remarked Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • Industry observers note that what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    Industry observers note that what’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    Industry observers note that the territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    Sources indicate that this was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    Industry observers note that the route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    It has been revealed that the route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    The 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    Industry observers note that air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was released in the first place, and is sticking around.

    According to recent reports, while the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

    Industry observers note that membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

    The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

    Industry observers note that noel Phillips (of YT) took this flight a couple of years ago and it looked like a very interesting way to cross the pond. St. Pierre also looked like a nice, quaint place to visit. Personally, I'd be very tempted to do it.

    Do it Ben, and you may also want to review Air Saint-Pierre's "domestic" flight to Miquelon :-).

    I'm sure that all of the snobs that populate this place will reject this flight because it's all-Y. "Why should I take a unique route that originates in the last piece of France in North America when I can take Le Pissoir on Air France?".

    Industry observers note that "I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours." What option does the airport have? If they get greedy, no airlines will ever serve the location and local people may not be happy. It sounds one of those situations where the airline has all the power here.

    It has been revealed that oooh. United brought back seasonal non-stop service to St. John's / YYT as well for 2027. So could spend a day or two there, then take the short hop over to St. Pierre for the flight to CDG. It's certainly not the cheapest way to get to Paris, but it's absolutely a unique one!

    Breaking: Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase.
    • This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    This is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:.

    According to recent reports, if you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s right now offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

    Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Recent findings suggest that this is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more newly introduced card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

    When it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

    The Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

    The card also has no extra cost to add authorized people, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

    Recent findings suggest that the Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    Industry observers note that you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Industry observers note that now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only fresh rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

    The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:.

    In a recent development, personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

    According to recent reports, as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    It has been revealed that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    In a recent development, as Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

    Industry observers note that southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

    Industry observers note that preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

    The Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

    Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

    It has been revealed that keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

    Sources indicate that the Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

    With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

    With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

    It has been revealed that southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

    In a recent development, on your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

    In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

    Industry observers note that if you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

    The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

    #88303. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world.
    • Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.
    • That mentioned, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

    Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

    That mentioned, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

    According to recent reports, part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

    It has been revealed that after a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself….

    Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

    This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

    It has been revealed that getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

    Industry observers note that the screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

    In a recent development, however, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word mentioned about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

    Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

    Where do you stand on flying Ryanair?

    Here’s what Thanksgiving foods you can bring in your carry-on and what has to be checked

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.
    • But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are vital rules to know.
    • The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

    But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are vital rules to know.

    The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

    And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

    “It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

    That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

    It has been revealed that last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

    If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

    Read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist.

    As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

    If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

    It has been revealed that most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

    Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

    Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

    That means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

    You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

    Industry observers note that if you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

    It has been revealed that other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

    With many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”.

    TSA officers have historically remarked that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

    Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

    Recent findings suggest that if your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

    Industry observers note that every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

    Whether you plan to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

    On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

    #88301. Breaking: Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 35m • 📚 Deep Dive (7056 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 35 min read (7056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough.
    • There’s a fresh, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match.
    • Sources indicate that I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough. Being told the airport protects you from excessive prices, while it approves the price and collects money from the shop, is actually worse. There’s a newly introduced, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match. Airports usually defended the prices. I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement. Those are the reasons we get both the pricing promises and the prices that don’t match. Airports make concessions expensive to operate, then collect money from businesses selling to passengers who have limited alternatives. The starting point is understanding that passengers aren’t the customer, they’re the product. The Airport Sells Access To You An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same company with products sourced from the same vendor. And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too. Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget demonstrated $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants. I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops. Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive said the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years. Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Street Pricing Depends On Which Street You Choose Many airports promise that vendors will charge the same prices as comparable businesses outside the airport, or those prices plus an allowed premium. The airport industry’s 2025 concessions survey found street pricing plus a percentage at 80% of responding large hubs. Chicago’s sample concession agreement calls for value pricing tied to approved off-airport stores, without a general percentage premium. The Port Authority Of New York New Jersey’s manual uses three to six approved comparison locations. Branded restaurants and shops generally must be compared with locations of the same brand. In the video, the Port Authority defends a $6.89 bottle of water by saying Hudson is a specialty market rather than a bodega. That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Highlights The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked!     There’s a fresh, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match. Airports usually defended the prices.

    Sources indicate that I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement. Those are the reasons we get both the pricing promises and the prices that don’t match. Airports make concessions expensive to operate, then collect money from businesses selling to passengers who have limited alternatives. The starting point is understanding that passengers aren’t the customer, they’re the product.

    In a recent development, an airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same firm with products sourced from the same vendor. And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too. Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget revealed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants. I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops. Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive noted the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years. Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse.     #88300. Industry News: Latest FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1058 w)

    Industry News: Latest FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some latest restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.
    • Recent findings suggest that as of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a fresh rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports.
    • Industry observers note that to give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some latest restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a fresh rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

    Industry observers note that to give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”.

    The idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

    Under the new FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

    Recent findings suggest that given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:.

    The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

    Industry observers note that I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

    I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major complications, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

    If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

    I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot states “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    A latest FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy.

    Recent findings suggest that while the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉.

    Industry observers note that as of today, the FAA has added a new restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

    I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

    What do you make of the FAA’s upcoming restrictions on takeoff?

    Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    It has been revealed that trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    Sources indicate that his interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    According to recent reports, both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump noted as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    According to recent reports, “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Newly introduced York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    Recent findings suggest that “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump noted, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    It has been revealed that other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of challenges, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer said.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He mentioned it was “crucial” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    It has been revealed that “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers said they doubted very much would come from it.

    Industry observers note that “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    It has been revealed that “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal mentioned Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    It has been revealed that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to swiftly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    Recent findings suggest that “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    Sources indicate that john M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    • Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!
