    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that bermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that debuted operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The company has just announced a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

    Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

    It has been revealed that for a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

    As I remarked from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

    In a recent development, to my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

    Industry observers note that several months back, BermudAir unveiled upcoming winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

    In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:.

    On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with new seasonal services in the following markets:.

    Below is BermudAir’s updated map with destinations listed….

    I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:.

    I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these fresh markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:.

    In a recent development, what’s interesting here is how the airline confirmed seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know….

    It’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

    BermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced newly introduced routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

    I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”.

    What do you make of BermudAir’s latest expansion?

A startup pivoting makes sense (all business class was always suspect), and shifting planes to destinations all over North America to connect various US/Canada passengers to various tropical destinations seems like a reasonable business model to me. I’m sure not all the dots and lines will work out, but I hope enough of them do!

    Upper Fresh England is growing....but you would think the flight from Portland would be in the winter. A nice way for those up north to get somewhere warm without connecting or going to Boston....

    Industry observers note that their planes have a proper domestic F cabin, not just a blocked middle. They're all E175s, so there are no middles at all.

    They apparently applied for Heathrow summer 2027 slots too, not sure what they were planning with those.

    Marriott’s Buena Park Grand Hotel & Suites promises “award-winning hospitality.” Guests rate it 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. A reader checked in and found stained bedding and a sofa he wouldn’t sit on. I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom. Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency. They didn’t always promise a lot, but they delivered exactly what they promised. The point of booking a chain was knowing what you’d get. You didn’t need to investigate eeach property to find out whether it met basic standards. You knew what the brand stood for. Now I find Marriott overpromises and enforces too little, afraid of alienating owners by making them spend money. Net rooms growth has become the priority, even when the rooms undermine the reason customers choose Marriott in the first place. Here, the property isn’t even flying one of Marriott’s flags yet and presumably there will be some investment. But they aren’t making the owner do that first, before delivering their guests. They’re trading a reputation built over decades for current fee revenue. Owners pay Marriott to deliver customers. If travelers stop trusting the company’s hotels, Marriott has fewer customers to send those owners. Then the owners have little reason to keep paying Marriott. Letting bad hotels stay in the system earns fee revenue from those properties today but sacrifices the ability of the chain to earn anything in the future. The Buena Park property is expected to transition to SpringHill Suites. Here’s a guest review from a reader with Lifetime Titanium status, who found Marriott asking $144.37 for the night. He paid less through Delta’s hotel booking portal. This is what he found. Marriott wanted $140 for a 1.6-star hotel Marriott wanted $144.37 a night for the Grand Hotel & Suites in Buena Park, California, an unbranded property that guests had rated 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. I booked it for less through Delta and found stains on the fitted sheet, red stains beneath a pillowcase and hair on a sofa I wouldn’t sit on. When you book a Marriott, you expect a Marriott. The whole point of having a hotel company’s name behind a reservation is that somebody has exercised a little judgment on your behalf. What judgment did Marriott International exercise here? The Grand is supposed to, at some point, become a SpringHill Suites by Marriott. When I arrived, I saw no Marriott signs. Some of the old signs and placards still noted Radisson. I paid $125.22 through Delta Air Lines’ hotel booking portal. With the branding up in the air, I couldn’t tell what Bonvoy benefits or points I’d receive for paying $144.37 to book directly with Marriott. Priceline would have saved me $13.25 over Delta, but I’d have missed out on the nearly 600 SkyMiles I earned. I arrived just after 2 p.m. The front desk clerk said my room was ready, but I’d have to pay $35 to check in before 3 p.m. I passed and came back a little more than an hour later. To be fair, I’d booked through a third party. Still, I gave the clerk my Bonvoy number at check-in. She never acknowledged my Lifetime Titanium Elite status or mentioned any benefits. I didn’t even get a bottle of water. The thing is, I liked the building. Its Spanish mission revival architecture was distinctive. You could also see where a restaurant and lounge had once been located. Whoever built the Grand clearly spent money on it. I suspect it was a great hotel in the early 1980s. More than four decades of neglect had, however, turned it into a dump. I booked a park-view suite with one king bed and one sofa bed. The view from my second-floor junior suite was of a parking lot and, beyond it, the main thoroughfare. At first glance, the room looked clean. Apart from the flooring and the one TV, I’d guess it had been 20 years since anything had been updated. Even the laminate flooring was peeling and torn. The toiletries in the bathroom were a mix of brands. The tub and shower had extensive patches of what looked like black mold. Then I looked at the sofa. There was hair and debris on it. One reason to book a suite is to have somewhere to sit besides the bed. That left the bed, where I found what appeared to be fluid stains on the bedding, including the fitted sheet. Under one pillowcase, the pillow protector had red stains of its own. The Grand fell well short of what I’d expect from a Quality Inn or a Ramada. I’d put it at what I expect from the nearby Motel 6. At Marriott’s rate of $144.37, staying here is highway robbery. I don’t believe for a minute this property would have made it into the chain in this condition when the Marriott family ran the company. I can imagine Bill Marriott saying, “Call us when the renovations are finished.” Arne Sorenson, the first CEO from outside the Marriott family, and his successor, Tony Capuano, ruined the brand the Marriotts built. SpringHill Suites is supposed to be one of Marriott’s better limited-service brands. It will be a long time before the Grand comes anywhere close to that standard.     Marriott wanted $140 for a 1.6-star hotel.

    Marriott wanted $144.37 a night for the Grand Hotel & Suites in Buena Park, California, an unbranded property that guests had rated 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website.

    I booked it for less through Delta and found stains on the fitted sheet, red stains beneath a pillowcase and hair on a sofa I wouldn’t sit on.

    When you book a Marriott, you expect a Marriott. The whole point of having a hotel tech giant’s name behind a reservation is that somebody has exercised a little judgment on your behalf. What judgment did Marriott International exercise here?

    According to recent reports, the Grand is supposed to, at some point, become a SpringHill Suites by Marriott. When I arrived, I saw no Marriott signs. Some of the old signs and placards still noted Radisson.

    It has been revealed that I paid $125.22 through Delta Air Lines’ hotel booking portal. With the branding up in the air, I couldn’t tell what Bonvoy benefits or points I’d receive for paying $144.37 to book directly with Marriott. Priceline would have saved me $13.25 over Delta, but I’d have missed out on the nearly 600 SkyMiles I earned.

    I arrived just after 2 p.m. The front desk clerk stated my room was ready, but I’d have to pay $35 to check in before 3 p.m. I passed and came back a little more than an hour later.

    To be fair, I’d booked through a third party. Still, I gave the clerk my Bonvoy number at check-in. She never acknowledged my Lifetime Titanium Elite status or mentioned any benefits. I didn’t even get a bottle of water.

    Sources indicate that the thing is, I liked the building. Its Spanish mission revival architecture was distinctive. You could also see where a restaurant and lounge had once been located. Whoever built the Grand clearly spent money on it. I suspect it was a great hotel in the early 1980s. More than four decades of neglect had, however, turned it into a dump.

    I booked a park-view suite with one king bed and one sofa bed. The view from my second-floor junior suite was of a parking lot and, beyond it, the main thoroughfare.

    At first glance, the room looked clean. Apart from the flooring and the one TV, I’d guess it had been 20 years since anything had been updated. Even the laminate flooring was peeling and torn. The toiletries in the bathroom were a mix of brands. The tub and shower had extensive patches of what looked like black mold.

    Then I looked at the sofa. There was hair and debris on it. One reason to book a suite is to have somewhere to sit besides the bed. That left the bed, where I found what appeared to be fluid stains on the bedding, including the fitted sheet. Under one pillowcase, the pillow protector had red stains of its own.

    The Grand fell well short of what I’d expect from a Quality Inn or a Ramada. I’d put it at what I expect from the nearby Motel 6. At Marriott’s rate of $144.37, staying here is highway robbery.

    I don’t believe for a minute this property would have made it into the chain in this condition when the Marriott family ran the firm. I can imagine Bill Marriott saying, “Call us when the renovations are finished.”.

    Arne Sorenson, the first CEO from outside the Marriott family, and his successor, Tony Capuano, ruined the brand the Marriotts built.

    Sources indicate that springHill Suites is supposed to be one of Marriott’s better limited-service brands. It will be a long time before the Grand comes anywhere close to that standard.

    Industry News: Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select Review—Why American Still Wins For Credit Card Spending Toward Status

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 44 min read (8899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~44 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • According to recent reports, american Airlines has the best overall U.S.
    • Sources indicate that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    According to recent reports, american Airlines has the best overall U.S. program for making credit card spending count toward status, and you don’t need one of its expensive premium cards to take advantage of it.

    Sources indicate that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap. You can combine those points with what you earn flying, shopping and through many of American’s other partners, all the way up to Executive Platinum. Meanwhile, the card’s checked bag benefit can cover its annual fee on a single family trip.

    I recently covered the card’s refresh, which adds Walmart+, an inflight credit and travel protections while raising the annual fee. Those changes take effect January 24, 2027. They improve the card for some customers, but the reason to put spending on it remains earning status.

    American’s current offer is 50,000 bonus miles after $2,500 in purchases within the first three months. There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months then $99, increasing to $150 with renewals starting January 24, 2027. That means for newly introduced applications, after the introductory year, the card’s annual fee is $150. Citi’s initial bonus restriction looks back 48 months. You aren’t eligible if you’ve received a Platinum Select new account bonus during that period, or converted another Citi card on which you earned a new account bonus during that period into a Platinum Select. A bonus on a different American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The miles are worth having. I’ve written about American’s partner award sweet spots, like 70,000 miles for business class between North America and the Middle East or Indian Subcontinent. And I find the miles useful for domestic travel too, often uncovering good mileage deals when cash prices are high (my sense that American doesn’t want to discount the fare, but doesn’t expect to fill the plane without doing so). Why American Is Best Overall For Spending Toward Status The card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels. Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses: AAdvantage Status   Loyalty Points   Card Spending Alone Gold   40,000   $40,000 Platinum   75,000   $75,000 Platinum Pro   125,000   $125,000 Executive Platinum   200,000   $200,000 American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway. The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades. Compare this with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier. Even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card. Alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit. What You Earn On Purchases The January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American currently charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized owners can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual plan, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after glitch and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee. What You Earn On Purchases The January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American currently charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized users can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual strategy, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to Newly introduced York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     Recent findings suggest that the card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels.

    Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses:.

    American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway.

    The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades.

    Industry observers note that compare this with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier.

    Industry observers note that even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card.

    Alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit.

For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     #88293. The House has a latest lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (702 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    The House has a latest lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.
    • It has been revealed that thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, said attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.

    It has been revealed that thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    According to recent reports, the House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    Recent findings suggest that "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-indicates; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    According to recent reports, johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    In a recent development, “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, noted. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    Sources indicate that “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., stated. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3175 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week.
    • Recent findings suggest that american Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar.
    • By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week. It’s still a shell, but the covered outdoor terrace is already there, and you can see the downtown skyline from the west end of the lounge. The new Admirals Club will have more than twice the space of the current one, and Austin is just one of the places where American is building bigger lounges. American Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar. And we’ll see both the renovated Washington National D concourse and replacement Chicago O’Hare L concourse clubs next year. By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well. The core and shell space is about to be turned over to American by the airport, allowing them to begin construction work. The current club is small. It was perfect-sized when I moved to Austin, but Austin has grown and overall American Airlines lounge visits have increased 80% over the past decade. Expectations for food have increased, too, and the kitchen facilities are inadequate. American is replacing its current club with a new one at the west end of the airport’s main concourse. In March, American Airlines confirmed the details of the blueprint for the new club above gate 35. More than 12,000 square feet (more than double the size of the current club) With an outdoor terrace and views of both downtown and airport operations. Supporting a gate allocation that’s expected to nearly double when the new terminal opens in the early 2030s. I keep looking at the space, waiting for progress, each time I fly out of the airport. I’m anxious for the new lounge! So far there are two renderings of the space that have been made available: Credit: American Airlines Credit: American Airlines This week I had a chance to peek inside the space, see the actual views from the space and the outdoor terrace. When you come up the elevator or walk up the stairs you’ll see the entrance – they’ll be taking down a preexisting wall there, and will install e-gates which are a new club standard (like at the Philadelphia A-West club – that location also has e-gates for the Flagship business class lounge, but that won’t be a standard). The kitchen will be at the far left, back of the lounge when you enter. The full kitchen facilities will allow in-house preparation for upgraded food. Closer, also to the left but nearer the windows will be the bar. At the opposite (west) end of the lounge, you can see out towards the downtown skyline. It gives some perspective on how small Austin’s downtown really is, though it’s far more dense than it was when I first moved here. The lounge’s outdoor deck has covering and shade, and American tells me it will have misters and fans – making it much more usable throughout the year. Living in Austin we eat outdoors much of the year, though the summers can get very hot and there will be days you don’t want to be outdoors between November and February. The former Chase Terrace on the opposite end of the airport lacked covering and climate assistance. Taking photos from the lounge is a bit challenging, because of the screens that the airport installs on the window meant for birds to be able to identify the glass and not fly into the building. Nonetheless, angle the lens just right and zoom past it and your photos can come closer to what you see out the windows (you really don’t see these screens except when you’re up close to the glass). American’s Austin gate allocation goes from 4 to 9 — a 125% increase – when the new concourse opens in the early 2030s. American can use common use gates in addition today. All nine of their dedicated gates will be on the current concourse, near this new lounge. Austin is part of a larger investment American is now making in its clubs. After several years where there wasn’t any growth in its network, and they even closed some lounges, here’s the American Airlines lounge pipeline: Airport Project Timing / status Austin New Admirals Club above the west gate expansion: more than 12,000 square feet, roughly double the current club, with an outdoor terrace. Permits issued, but American hasn’t announced an opening date. Expected at the end of 2027. Charlotte New Admirals Club above the airport atrium: more than 40,000 square feet, with showers, multiple bars and food stations. 2028 anticipated. Charlotte First Flagship Lounge, separately announced from the new Admirals Club. Size and opening date haven’t been disclosed. Chicago O’Hare Replacement Concourse L Admirals Club exceeding 10,000 square feet, with more seating and airfield views. Construction underway. Existing L club stays open during the work. No opening date announced. Dallas–Fort Worth New Terminal C Admirals Club: 37,000 square feet near the Skylink station. No opening date disclosed. Dallas–Fort Worth Terminal F Provisions by Admirals Club, the initial lounge offering in a broader premium-space program for the new terminal. Planned for Terminal F’s first phase. Later premium spaces and individual opening dates haven’t been shared. Miami New Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club. The current Flagship space becomes Admirals Club space, nearly doubling American’s total lounge footprint at the airport. No opening date disclosed. Nashville Replacement Admirals Club in the new Concourse A: about 17,400 square feet including outdoor terraces and an interior balcony, replacing the current roughly 7,000 square foot club. Construction expected to begin in 2027. No firm opening date announced. New York JFK Provisions by Admirals Club in Terminal 8: 3,700 square feet near gates 12–14, with hot and cold food, a dedicated barista bar and customer assistance. Targeted for December 2026. Phoenix Expansion and refresh of all three Terminal 4 Admirals Clubs. Near term work at A19–A21 improves food service. The B5–B7 club gets 20% more seats. Longer term, the two A clubs nearly triple their combined space and add approximately 150% more seats. Announced November 2026. No completion dates disclosed. San Antonio First Admirals Club in new Terminal C. Airport intends specify a 10,000 square foot American Airlines lounge. Documented by the airport, no formal American lounge announcement yet. Terminal C targets mid-2028, but no separate lounge opening date. Washington National Rebuilt Concourse D Admirals Club: more than 10,000 square feet and approximately 50% more seats. Expected to deliver in 2027. The real treat in Austin, though, isn’t the design or that there will be an outdoor deck – it’s the staff in the Austin club who are the absolute best in the system. They know the names of all regulars on sight and welcome you into the lounge. They work magic with itineraries – and they keep working that magic even once you’ve left, frequently bird dogging inventory and improving connections even after you’ve left the lounge. When I’ve had flights cancelled and could only get a long connection in Dallas or Charlotte, I’ve found myself landing to notes saying they’ve gotten me on an earlier flight because space opened up. They do this for everyone. It’s a small city, personal customer service feel even in a growing market. And that makes Admirals Club membership (and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] cardmembership) worth it. The Austin club space will finally match the service once this lounge opens. I genuinely cannot wait for the lounge to open because it’ll make flying American Airlines out of my home airport that much better.     #88291. Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (980 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Solarpowerworldonline ↗ Open Full Page

    Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects.
    • A residential solar project in Newly introduced York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions.
    • According to recent reports, after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the One Major Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

    A residential solar project in Newly introduced York installed by Nickels Energy Solutions. Credit: Nickels Energy Solutions.

    According to recent reports, after 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial company, and not the homeowner.

    Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central Fresh York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

    “We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” said Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”.

    Sources indicate that TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

    These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

    Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

    It has been revealed that “I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”.

    Selling residential solar in 2026.

    Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the manufacturer’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

    Despite that, Wright mentioned he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

    Wright-Way Solar built a solar plus storage project at a Ranch in Texas featuring arrays that are facing east, west and south. Credit: Wright-Way Solar.

    “I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my manufacturer and the industry more than the customer,” Wright mentioned. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”.

    Industry observers note that tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

    That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

    “Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright remarked.

    In a recent development, NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in Upcoming York. Nickels noted that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

    Sources indicate that “The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels said. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”.

    It has been revealed that some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states at the moment have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

    It has been revealed that while traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to newly introduced grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

    “We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

    Industry News: Ryanair Flew 208 Million Passengers At An Average Fare Of $56—Now Its Rivals Want It Grounded For Not Being European Enough

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly.
    • European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares.
    • In a recent development, the European Network Airlines Association claims it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly. Their objection is to who owns the airline that carried 208 million passengers at an average fare of just €51 in the year ended March 31. European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares. Competitors say they run afoul of foreign ownership rules, but those European investors exercise 100% voting control of the ariline. I don’t see Europe grounding Ryanair. I do see why its competitors might like want to pick this fight. The European Network Airlines Association says it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules. That didn’t get them what they wanted so they sued the Irish Aviation Authority. On November 16, the judge declined to add Lufthansa, Air France and KLM as parties to the case, though they can submit affidavits. A hearing is scheduled for December 16. Who Owns Ryanair, And Who Gets Control? Brexit turned British shareholders into foreign investors without anybody having to sell a share. Since January 2021, nonqualifying shareholders haven’t been allowed to attend, speak or vote at Ryanair shareholder meetings. On March 7, 2025, Ryanair let them buy ordinary shares in Dublin again. It kept the voting ban, including for any votes the chairman might otherwise cast on their behalf. Ryanair says the change opened the door to inclusion in stock indexes. Its board said it would restrict purchases again if European ownership fell to 20%. . At both March 31 and September 30 this year, Ryanair put qualifying European ownership at 30%. That includes investors from Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Shares held through its U.S. depositary are generally non-qualifying. Here’s who shows up in Ryanair’s March 31 shareholder disclosure. Reported holder    Share of Ryanair Capital Group 14.6% MFS 4.7% Artisan Partners 4.5% Michael O’Leary 4.0% BlackRock 4.0% Fidelity 3.3% By October, Capital Group reported 15.70% for client accounts, and T. Rowe Price reported 3.00%. O’Leary’s 4% economic stake translates to 13% voting control. Does It Matter More Who Owns The Shares Or Who Controls The Airline? European law requires both. Qualifying states or their nationals have to own more than half the airline and effectively control it. Giving Europeans every vote solves the legal glitch of control. The key legal question here is whether shares that carry no voting rights count as equity for the ownership test. European regulators have allowed this in the past. Wizz Air says British and Hungarian regulators approved its plan to suspend some foreign shareholders’ votes after Brexit so Wizz Air Hungary could keep its European license. easyJet just did this in a takeover vote. When shareholders approved an Apollo deal on November 11, qualifying Europeans owned 35.07% of easyJet. It suspended voting rights on 233,921,894 shares. Those shareholders keep their dividend rights. The proposed deal itself caps Apollo’s ordinary equity at 49.9%. But this is complicated. A 1995 Swissair–Sabena decision found that Swissair held 49.5% of the Belgian airline’s voting shares, plus special certificates that the European Commission agreed to leave out of the ownership calculation. Those certificates had no votes, generally paid at least 5% and gave Swissair no share of the assets left over in liquidation. That looked like debt. In contrast, a Ryanair shareholder who can’t vote still collects dividends (which aren’t fixed) and gains or loses money on fluctuations of the stock. What Happens If Ryanair Loses? If all the ordinary shares count, Ryanair has to get qualifying ownership above 50%. That’s 207 million existing shares moving from non-European to European owners (assuming they don’t issue latest shares). The airline’s articles of incorporation allow it to direct restricted holders to sell to qualifying investors. This is being framed in some quarters as Ryanair having to shut down. That doesn’t seem likely. I’ve been writing about foreign airline ownership since 2003. If someone abroad is willing to put up the money for more planes and cheaper flights, what does the passenger gain by turning them away? If Europe needs aircraft and crews available for defense, it can pay airlines to provide them. Forcing a British retiree to sell Ryanair stock to a Frenchman doesn’t add aircraft that Europe can use for its defense. It does, however, give Lufthansa and Air France a way to raise a competitor’s cost of capital. So it’s decent return on trade association dues.     #88289. Tech Report: Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (623 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Sources indicate that rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    Industry observers note that in a statement McIver remarked she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver remarked in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    Recent findings suggest that the criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    According to recent reports, earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of Fresh Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

  • JetBlue's TrueBlue loyalty program offers flexible points earning and redemption, with no blackout dates for JetBlue-operated flights.
  • Points can be earned through flights, partner activity, shopping portals, and transferable rewards, and do not expire.
  • The program features Points Pooling, allowing groups to combine balances, and a tiered elite status system with benefits that increase at higher levels.
  • TrueBlue's expanding partner network, including a new partnership with United, enhances both earning and redemption options.
  • JetBlue uses a revenue-based model, so points required for flights typically reflect cash prices, and partner award availability may be limited.

    #88287. Breaking: Delta Flight Attendants May Get Their First Union Vote Since 2010 — But Saying Yes Could Mean Smaller Paychecks

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 33m • 📚 Deep Dive (6515 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Delta Flight Attendants May Get Their First Union Vote Since 2010 — But Saying Yes Could Mean Smaller Paychecks

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6515 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play.
    • AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson says she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines.
    • Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play. It can be a useful stalking horse, where the airline pays up generously to keep its crew from unionizing. But once they actually pull the trigger, there’s little reason – or ability – to continue paying above industry wages. AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson notes she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines. Brian Sumers came away from their November 12 interview at the Skift Aviation Forum thinking she’ll get an election and win it. A vote in 2027 is a real possibility. If I were Delta crew I’d vote no. The union would get about 30,000 flight attendants to represent. Crews who already get better than what other airline unions bargain for could wind up taking home less. Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%. The National Mediation Board needs valid cards from at least half the eligible flight attendants, and a card more than a year old won’t count. Delta organizers put the minimum at roughly 15,000 signatures. Once there’s an election, a majority of valid votes cast decides it. Nelson also noted she was months away in 2024. Later that November organizers said they were weeks from having the cards. Delta flight attendants have rejected representation three times, but the vote after the Northwest merger was close. In 2010, 9,544 voted against representation and 9,216 voted for it. Sumers says he hears more confidence from Nelson this time. She can pick when to file, and a loss would normally mean waiting a year to try again while cards expire. If Nelson files with a comfortable cushion above the threshold, that would give her the edge in an election. Delta’s Pay Advantage Is Profit Sharing American Airlines and United Airlines now pay slightly higher hourly rates at the top of the flight pay scale. It’s $86.32 per flight hour at Delta, $87.04 at American and $87.47 at United. At 80 flight hours a month, United’s $1.15 advantage is about $1,100 a year in base pay.For newer hires, Delta starts a little higher than both. But Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year. Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a upcoming hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026. United got boarding pay in its new deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. . The Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants. Union Flight Attendants Go A Long Time Between Raises Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the new contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. The National Mediation Board can release the parties from mediation, normally starting a 30 day cooling off period before the union can strike or the airline can impose new terms. In practice that hasn’t happened for flight attendants since 1993. Nelson said at Skift that she wants more frequent bargaining to deliver smaller, more regular raises. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers.     AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson says she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines. Brian Sumers came away from their November 12 interview at the Skift Aviation Forum thinking she’ll get an election and win it. A vote in 2027 is a real possibility. If I were Delta crew I’d vote no. The union would get about 30,000 flight attendants to represent. Crews who already get better than what other airline unions bargain for could wind up taking home less.

    #88284. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks
